blocks.x: Bill Russell 1868 in 1961. Do you mind giving your full name?
You said you were working here in town? What were you doing here in town?
Well, I was working construction work. Oh, I see. Yeah.
I worked for a fellow pretty good while. And you were playing at just the night time?
Night time, yeah.
Did you play during the week or just the weekends?
Oh, no. Sometimes we get jobs in the week. We play them. Not going to get a job any day. Pay more than my job for waking up. I'd stop and go play that job.
Yeah, sure.

That's true. Some little job, like you used to call them bonques. It didn't play but two dollars, but I don't care why. I was waking up. I would knock off and go play that bonques for the partner you have. Most of them. Oh, man, them dinners. Oh, yeah. Lots to eat, huh? Oh, yeah. You had plenty of fun. You had nothing strong but you had this, what do you call this? Nail beer. Nail beer? Nail, nail. Not no nail.
Oh, yeah. During Prohibition, yeah. Yeah. Something like two-thirds of one percent. All like that.
Something like we did. I don't know. I'm telling you, we used to have the time.
Would you play out in the open at those bonques? No, it used to be in the hall.
Oh, the hall. Yeah.
All everyone operated was in the hall.

Oh, like a dance hall. Yeah. The cooperators, perseverance, new hall, sometimes the economy. That's what they, that's them old societies. Yeah. That's what they call their anniversary. They call them bonkers. Every year they'd have them the same day time.
That's right.
That's right. Well, then you'd, would you play and then eat later or? So, they are usually stopped at 12 o'clock. As soon as you get there, before you hit a tune, then you could go get your dinner.
That's at 12 o'clock noon?

Yeah. Go ahead and get your gumbo and your chicken stew. Chicken gumbo and chicken stew. And partner used to feed. That is good. Then you go up and you play, you might play about an hour, hour and a half. Or you would get another little snack of going and refresh it. It was really good. You could play till five o'clock. I had to get two dollars for it. I don't care why I was waking. When they had one of them, I was waking. I quit. Yeah. I quit and go to that tune.
I was going to ask some more about that band I mentioned before that you played in the Piku. Oh. And Milton, Mr. Milton was telling us about just two days ago.
Well, that was, that was the last band I played in. Piku had a piece there, it was called Get Busy Right. Get Busy Right.
Get Busy Right. Yeah. Just went something like that.

Do you hear it? Do you hear it? Do you hear it? Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada Dada D Yeah, I come in with the trombone.
That is at the very end? The little trombone bar?
Yeah. I put a ear in. It's been so long. It's been hard. It's been hard. It's been hard. It's been hard. It's been hard. It's been hard. Then my mind is all so far and I know I just lose my wife.
Yes, I remember I was at the wake. Oh, that's right. You see you at the wake.
About two or three weeks ago. Yeah. On Blandin's. At Blandin's. Yeah, it was Easter Saturday. I mean Good Friday.
Yeah. Right over there. Sheik. We just saw Sheik walking over there by the corner here a minute ago.
Yeah. If he knew you was coming there, he already came with you.

He was on the way to George Gano. He said he had to be there. He was the one to take him some papers and try some numbers with him. So he was in a hurry to run over. He would have stopped there. Did Piku have many other pieces that he wrote that you know of in those days? Did he have many other numbers by him or was that the only one that you remember that he wrote?
Well, he rearranged a couple of records. No, the record come from me. He rearranged some records.

I wonder if you don't mind, due to that noise there with all of those cars, I'm not sure that it picked up that tune very well. And I'd like to be able to hear it sometime. If you don't mind, we can point this maybe a little bit, get it up a little closer to you. And if you don't mind humming it, I don't like to make it do all that over again. But I'm not sure it's on there real clear. If you don't mind, the tune again of Piku's. And I'll hold this mic up a little closer to you.
You see that's why he makes the run on the planet. That was your trombone part at the end. Sort of like a break at the end. Yeah, that's the break you used to get at the end.
Did they all come in for one final note there?
When I make... When I... That was the last.
I think I'll leave this mic sit right up here. It'll pick up. You don't have to face it there. It'll pick you up all right. It's a little better there.
Well, what... About what year was that when you were playing that with Piku?
I'll give you that. That was about 19... Between 30 and 32.
That was your last band that you played in, huh?
Yeah.
Can you tell us some more about Chris Kelly? I understand you played with him quite a few years.
Oh yeah. I played with him longer than I did any band.
What kind of a trumpet was he and what kind of a leader? I never did know him at all and he didn't make any records so we don't know much about him.
No, well... He's a pretty good ragtime corner player.
Who else was in the band too while you were there?

Well a fellow by the name of... Mealy Bong that was one of his old... Yeah, we know him. ...clanet players. And then... Peter Patton used to play... Banjo. And then Marrero boys, one named Lounge, he playing bass. I want to say guitar. Yeah. The banjo there. Yeah, Lawrence played. Played banjo. And Eddie, he played bass. Oh yeah.
He's still living. He's still around. Yeah.
And Faiso, drummer, well he played drum with us some. We had Big Willie Phillip, Bill Phillip, well he played drums some. We had several drum players.
Faiso, was that his real name or was it that his name?
No, that's all I know is Faiso. But he was a hell of a drummer.
Really good.
Yeah, I think he left with me and I never know what happened to him.
I never did see him.
Didn't someone, someone that spoke to you concerned that?
I've heard the name but I never knew much about it.
But he was a good drummer. That's indeed. He's definitely, he never did come back.
Can you tell us more about Chris Kelly now? What kind of a fellow was he? I don't even know if he was big or little or light or dark or what did he look like?
Oh, he was a kind of dark brown skin fellow. Well, he didn't dress so well. He was really bad also right.
Feral House type, was that the type he played the music to?
Yeah, he played the ball of music.
They say he used a lot of mutes.
I heard he used a mute and was good on the blues.

Oh, on that Floyd's thing there. The rubber plunger. Yeah. Oh, I used to like that you ain't play, I mean Kelly's Love. He put that up there. Wah wah wah wah wah wah wah wah wah wah wah wah wah wah wah wah wah wah wah wah wah wah wah. I'm telling you, he was good on that Kelly's love. I don't believe nobody here could beat him. I read Kelly's love.
And what would you play on your trombone as an accompaniment to? Did you use loops in your trombone?

Sometimes, no I never didn't use that. I'd put a mat, put a derby, or a hat over my arms, and play behind it. He was a good street man. In them days used to have some advertising. You get out on the street with a truck, you better be right. Don't a guy run you all over town. I remember one Sunday, this must have been about two o'clock, our band and Rene met there on Roman Street. We stayed there from two until after five.
And that one class?
Right there. One band wouldn't move. Chris told a fellow if we move in there, he'd get out. You'd get out. So we finished our advertising right there.
With Rene, yeah? Yeah. Who won? Did anybody tell who they thought was best?
It was the crowd, you see. Some guy pulled for Chris, but Rene had to pull a good pull over there because he used to live there on Cornice Street. That was only a couple of blocks from his house.
All his friends were there.
Yeah. We had some friends around there too. Did Chris know many different pieces
or did he stick mostly to blues? People tell me he was very good on blues. Did he know a lot of other numbers too? Or what all did you play in the band? How many numbers?
Well he used to play different numbers, but Chris had several blues there. He used to have blues, I don't get how they go, but he used to call it the Three Sixes.
Three Sixes?
Mm-hmm. Yeah. And that was the blues though. Yeah.
One that he made up himself I guess. Yeah.

Let's see how he used to call it. Ta ta ta ta ta ta ta. Oh wow wow wow wow wow wow. He was good all right. He used to call it. It's been so long now I don't remember because I had no... I used to know all them things, but it's done flipped me now. I've been putting him in 30 years.

Well that gives us a good idea of his style. That's better than most people. Most people just say, well he used one of the flushers and they played blues and that's all they tell us. Well he used to play other pieces,
but his hobby was blues. He was the right time cornet player. That's all of his story. To my judgment he was good. I played the last job with him on earth.
Where was the last job? Do you remember?
McDonnellville.
Up in McDonnell.
Yeah. Couldn't walk from near to that door unless he had to stop. He was very sick? Yeah, when he was just that short. Now his heart was bad. The heart that's give out on him.
He wasn't a very old man was he?

No, Chris was around about 38 years old when he died. He was old. Yeah. Me and him was around about the same age. Because we used to kid one another all the time. About our age. So you know he was about that age then.
Yeah.
Actually how many years you went back footed down there by Ironton. That's why he come from a little farm that's called Ironton down the coast. It was down near the Magnolia Plantation.
That's right. That's right. St. Henry and Jim Robinson.
That's right. Some of those. Yeah. But he was just a little bit further than Magnolia. Further down the river. Yeah. He was the place where he was Ironton.
Yeah. I never knew it was very good. We talked to his brother Ben Kelly is still there. Yeah. Maybe he told us I forgot. He told us where he was born.
Oh I beg your pardon. He wasn't quite full as son Henry was from Magnolia. Yeah. But he was between Magnolia and this other big farm he had got down there. I just remember.
Jim says he came from Deer Range I think.
Yeah. Yeah. That's where him and Chris all them came from the same place.
Yeah. Down the same locality.
Yeah. On the same little farm. Yeah. They always, all of them were together because they had a little band down there.
Well I think of it. Did you ever see a picture of Chris Kelly? I've never seen a picture of him. That's why I didn't know what he looked like even.
He kind of resembled me because we used to pass for crumbles.
He wasn't as big as you though I bet was he? Yeah. Was he? I didn't know he was tall.
Yeah.
I always pictured him.
He was about five foot ten.
I always thought maybe he was a little fella.
I was like.
Mm-mm. I guess Buddy Petit was real little.
Oh now that's the little, that was the little man. Buddy Petit and Rene. Yeah. Them was little fellas.
I saw Rene, I remember he's small.
Mm-hmm.
I had the idea Chris Kelly was small too.
But he wasn't. No, I know. Chris was a big heavy guy. Oh I didn't know. Mm-hmm. That's a big husker.

Can I go to the water? Mm-hmm. Now where old did you play? You mentioned that last job you played. Where was the, uh, is it in a hall or an organization or what? It was in the hall. In the hall. Just across the river then. Just across the river. Just across the river then. Just across the river. Remember any of the other main jobs you had? Did you ever play any regular engagements? That is every week the same place or anything?

Bulls. The Bulls Aiden Pleasure Club. Mm-hmm. Up there on 8th Street. Yeah. We played there about, see, two seasons. Every week about? Every Tuesday. Every Tuesday. Yeah. That's a Bulls Aiden Pleasure Club.
Well that's the Elks that took that over now.
Oh yeah. I don't, the money them people made, I don't see how they lost it. Make plenty of money. Every Tuesday night the place feels like packing jam. Sometime they have two bands. Oh yeah.
That's right. One on each end of the hall?
Yep. They had, they had, right under the basement that was the hall. On Ramport Street side you had a lawn there. Drive Street side you had a lawn over there.
I see a lawn. Yeah. Well I remember there's a big yard up there now. Yeah. Yeah.
I don't tell you, no place used to be packed.
You say Chris and Chris and you used to kid together, what did he have a good sense of humor? Was he a nice fella. Jolly sort of father?
Yeah. Nice fella. Nice fella.
He's sort of, not likely to lose his temper or something.

Well he was kind of hard headed but he could be easily conked down. Yeah. Cause I used to conk him plenty of times. But one thing I didn't like about him, he used to fool with your money so much. Yeah. In them days you always sign a contract and they give you a deposit. Oh yeah, I've heard of that. Now if you wouldn't be there with Chris, Chris would take that deposit and meet a couple of them little nitbit and get in his feet and drink it all up.
Yeah.

He's time for pity now. Some of the men, that's why his band is going to get short. But I used to manage to get up soon in the morning and catch him. When he started going out, we'd go together. Yeah, that's what you do. So when he get his deposit, I'll be ready to get mine. Yeah. Well he used to like me all right. Cause he used to follow one another. I should be with him every day. See I wasn't waking in the day then. I quit waking over there.
By the way, do you know what kind of a horn he used? Is the carnet trumpet or short carnet or what did it look like?
When Chris died, Chris had with them one of them little bit of gold carnet, just about that long.
Gold man?
Mm-hmm. One of them little bit of carnet.
So he never did use a big long carpet then?

No. Chris used to pawn his strong so much. He used to pawn it all the time anyway. Yeah, when he died that was his phone. Yeah. Oh boy. He didn't know what he did with his money. He had to use a bugle with crape on it at his tomb. That's where he had to represent his trumpet or bugle.
That was, where was that? Was it his funeral you said? Yeah.
Did he have a band when he was buried, do you remember? Yeah, three bands.
Three bands.
Yeah. I heard about Buddy Petit's funeral. I think they had a big one.
Yeah, they had a band, one band.
I never heard about Chris Kelly's funeral much.
Man, you're the same as carnival around here when they buried Chris Kelly. There was Chris Kelly. I think Chris Kelly, Black Benny, Shiller Stein, Piku. He had more than anyone else.
There was four of the biggest funerals you can remember. Yeah, with the musicians.
Yeah.
Yeah.
That's the G. It's around the same as people lined up side to side walk, the same as a carnival.
Where did Chris Kelly live about in those days? What part of town?
Well, he used to live there on Liberty Street. When he died, he was living on Liberty Street.
Down near the old Cooperators Hall and that section about?

Right off from the auditorium. But he done tore that house down. That's why he died after. Yeah, right near the auditorium. Yeah, but he used to live different, but he lived over the basement. Yeah, and yeah, wasn't there too long, no way.
By the way, where did you live when you moved to town? What part of town did you live in?
When I first came here, I moved up on Ramport Street, rumming up 1131.
Your fellow city along in that section of?
No, just near Contoy. Not Contoy, Clio. Yes, I remember.
Yeah, because the car used to go back there. And that's when you took lessons from Dave Perkins uptown? Dave Perkins, yeah.
Yeah, I lived in the room then.
Well, I think of Dave Perkins again. Was he playing in any band in those days or just teaching?
Teaching, he used to play with white bands.
That's right, I heard he played with Jack Lane, Papa Lane they call him sometimes.
Yeah, yeah, he played with white bands.
Even in those days he was playing with white bands.
Yeah. His wife was colored, but he looked like white to me.
That's what everybody says, he's very likely.

Yeah. And I moved from, when I got me a little bit of a foothold, I got me a house back on, on Durbinet. Between Thalia and Malcolm H. I stayed there about a year, then after that in 21 I moved down here. And I've been reading this percentage ever since.
Right, right in this section? Yeah. Well, did you play any brass band work in those years when you were working with Chris? Did he ever play brass band?
Yeah, I used to, sure, he used to play a few.
With Chris's band then, was he the leader or?

Yeah, he'd be the leader, but we'd pick up men, you see. Pick up anybody? Anybody. Yeah. That's how I would. He'd pick up like the guy well known if he'd get killed or die. Well, they had fellas going around, one by the name, Ernest, Prince, Taki, or Jerry. Well, they'd go around and pick up. What's the name of they'd pick up? He'd carry to Chris and we'd play a few.
Yeah. Those guys would be like agents for Chris, would they? They'd pick up the work?

Well, sometimes they'd give it to Chris and they'd give it to other fellas, but Chris and Rodenapp had it. Because if he didn't pick up too much, little, well, Chris would play for that little. Sometimes I could borrow two dollars, a man. Well, Chris would play for it. Well, if he'd pick up the real funeral price in them, they'd assume it was three dollars a man. But he'd play it more so.
Did you play a funeral watchie? Did you play them from music or did you play them? Oh, no.
We could just drum what we used to play. We could play that from here. What a friend we have with Jesus.
Mostly some hymns.
Yeah. Oh, it's all hymns. Never Oh My God to See. All like that.
Do you remember in those days that they used, some of the ones they use today are by and by. Did they use that?
That's right.
What about Just a Closer Walk with the...
Walk with Jesus. That's right. See? Yeah.
Just a Closer Walk. Did they use that along that road?
Sure. See, all that's old stuff.
I think it was real old.
Yeah.
And what about the saints go marching in? They claim that so much now. Was that an old... Did that just come popular lately or was it used?
Well, it was popular in my time. We'd be coming back. You used that?
Yeah. Another one that they use now is the Glory Land and Sing On. Oh, yeah.
All that. All that's that old stuff.
You used all those old numbers then? That's right.
The Eureka band play...
Now they play... Was it Flea the Bird? Well, that's a march. That's a funeral march. I remember that.

Did you ever play funeral marching? Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. I played with a guy across the river and he had a funeral you'd better know how to read when you go there. Oh, yeah. That was old man Henry Allen. Oh, yes.
You played Henry Allen's band then, too. You heard him, man. Yeah, he had nothing but real funeral march.

Yeah. Yeah. Flea the Bird. I done played at him many times. Oh, then, didn't he ramble? That was Chris' place when he turned you loose when he coming back. That was his piece. Didn't he ramble? Rambles come to put his cutting down. Well, did he, I got to get a piece of music. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Well, did he, I guess he wouldn't use his boots on a parade.
Oh, not for no parade, no. Uh-uh. Need all the air you could get in there for a parade.
Now, was he a pretty big-tone loud or was he soft on the praise?
No, he was a kind of stark player, a connet player. Pretty big-tone. Yeah. Yeah. He was kind of stark.
But he, I suppose for dances he'd come down soft sometimes? Oh, yeah.

Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. You had to come down. I didn't like that kind of riff. Blowing your head off all the way through. Coming with some kind of harmony. Yeah. Yeah. Get down low. Did you have more than one cornet in the marching band? Yeah, we had three. About how big a band did you have on the street? Well, we had some dear to dear to dear to dear to dear to dear dear dear dear dear dear Let's see, we have three cornet players, a clarinet, two drums, two trombones, a ballotone, and a bass.
Remember who was played with you in those bands more than anyone?
I know you say a lot of different people, but the...
Oh yeah, we speak of different fellas.
Who were some of the main ones that Chris liked to use?
George Hook across the river.
Oh yeah, carnet was he?
No, he was a baritone.
Oh, baritone, yeah.
I forget that old man, he used to play with the exultures, bass. Chris used to like them two fellas. He'd always get them.
What was his name, the bass player?
I can't think of his name, it's been so long.
Not Jackson?
No, he used to play with Manuel Forrest, exultures.
Oh, it would be Tats Alexander.

No, he was a ballastone. It wouldn't be old Joe Howard played. No, he used to play bass. Sometime on the last, he used to hit Joe Howard, because Joe Howard was playing in a bass in our orchestra. Oh, he did. That's when they quit bass violin all together in some of the years back. That's when they used them bass. He used the tuba. Yeah.
Who was his favorite son clarinet? Who did he like to use on clarinet?

Well, he used to get this little fella, George Lewis. He was the only lad, George Lewis. He used to play with him all the time. That's what George told me he played since then. Yeah. And he used to use the solo for what he used to play with bass drum, what he used to play with Ben and Tippet or Clay. Clay. Oh, yeah. Giles. Yeah, I want to say Giles.
Clay Giles. Clay Giles.

Yeah, he was a drummer too. Because he used to play with the solstice down here. Well, did you know them up there too, the Giles? I know him from Tippet or the little kid. Well, that one died out there by the name of Albert Giles. Yeah, there were several of them, yeah. Yeah, even Albert got a little son down here.
And his boy still playing. Yeah, he was playing the same thing with his daddy. He used to play.
Yeah, he was playing. Same thing with his daddy.
He used to play.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. That's a young dude. Yeah. Sometime I worked with him but I never just play in his band. I used to play extra sometimes. Yeah. Exactly. And we used to hire him plenty of time. But with this little band here or this last band I played, Ernest Milton.
Did you ever work with Buddy Petey?

Yeah, sometime I worked with him, but I never just played in his band. I used to play extra sometimes. And we used to hire him plenty of times. But with this little band here, this last band I played, Ernest Milton. Buddy was playing second con with Ernest Milton when he died. Buddy was supposed to go with him, a place down there he used to call it Burwood. Used to go down there and play with him. Well that job coming up that Saturday, well he'd take him sick because he didn't stay sick alone just one day.
He died in a sudden.

Yeah, he died in a sudden. Well if they went to see him that morning, you told him wait a minute he'll be able to go. Well he waited there and he wasn't getting no better so he went on down. When they come back, he was dead. He died that Saturday night. And at the time he died his friend was Louis Armstrong.
Well I remember they had, he was the...
Paul Barrow.
Yeah, the honorary Paul Barrow or something on the... Yeah, I remember reading about it. Louis wrote about it in his book.

Mm-hmm. It has a fine little second tone that that boy had. Buddy Picky. He talked about a harmony in the horn. He had it. He kind of gave Louis Armstrong plenty of ideas when Louis was down here. But Louis used to play on the street down here. Yes, I heard he did.

I think it was the Tuxedo Band, I believe. Mm-hmm. Did you ever play at the Tuxedo Grass Band or... Not in them days, no. The Onward Grass Band, Emmanuel Perez, ever? No, I didn't play with them. I might ask, we only have another minute or so on this tape, but who were your favorite trombonists? You mentioned Frankie Doosen and any others that you liked real well?

Yeah, I got a couple of young fellas under them, a little fella by the name of Moise French. Used to play with Rene. I've heard of him, I never heard of him. Yeah, I find he was a sweet little trombone player. We had another little fella that you played some nice trombone. He used to play with a little fella that's called Clayton. I forget that boy's name. Did you ever interview Clayton? No, not yet.
We'll do that pretty soon. Yeah, well... I know him very well.
He had a little trombone player. Them come up wrong in my class, I find he was pretty good.
Clayton will tell us about him when we talk to him.
Yeah.
Sure can know his name.
Yeah, he's...
Anything else you'd like to tell about the bands you played with?
I played with another band up there. We used to call him Kid Nicholas. We called him Wooden Jones.
Oh, yes.

That guy was like a mule. That guy could take a brass band out on the street by himself. Powerful. Yes, he used to call him Wooden Joe, and he was Wooden Joe too. Yeah, he was powerful. I played with his band a pretty good while. That was a dance band there?
Yeah, he had to dance.

I told him Kid Nick. We had Keon Cornette. I was on trombone. Israel Garment used to play clarinet. A fellow by the name of Lucky used to live up in Carrollton. He used to play bass. Arthur Roden. Arthur Roden. . . .

You were talking about Wooden Joe. I'm not sure we got all of the men on. The drummer, who was the drummer with Wooden Joe? Arthur Hogan. Oh yes. And the banjo? John Smith. I think we got the others. Did you mention any bass player? Yeah, we used to call him Buddy Lux. I forget his right name, but we used to call him Buddy Lux.

About where did you play? What kind of jobs? I mean, were they? We used to dance, picnics. Single spot jobs all around? Yeah, all around. We had no particular place. The longest place we played was up on Hickory and Eagle. We used to call that place the merry-go-round. We used to play up there every Monday night. Yeah, we played up there about two seasons. Every Monday night.
You say Wooden Joe was so powerful, did you play with him on the street too sometime?

I'm telling you, somehow on the street up here we used to one guy. He hired a couple of corner players and if they ain't there any time to leave, he'd leave out there by himself. That was one powerful man. I heard him too. I even made some records once with him and he was even powerful over the last few years of his life. He had a lot of power. Well, now he would've known when he was the way in the time when I'm talking about. He wasn't tough. That's a man just used to blow up. He didn't know a note of as big as that lamp up there. He was called a man. He used to blow up. He used to blow up. He had to run it, that's it. When he was under a piece and it didn't take him too long to run it either. He played over once or twice and he'd come back there and he'd put in your gutcha.
Did you ever play any advertising jobs with him at all?

Yeah, I used to play at the mayor go around. Sometime he'd come up there and we'd run across a couple of bands around there. I'm telling you. We used to shake them up. We'd run across a bunch. We'd have caught him. That's why you said something about the records. I don't know if I just killed a look. I'm more sure my wife got a book there of Bunk.

I'd like to look over and see if you have any records that you'd sell. I'm done. Some of those we might be able to use up at Tulane too. We have quite a few. I don't know. You've got pretty good eyes, y'all. Yes, if you have a candy. My eyes are so bad. Well, I think, did you ever make any records yourself? Did you ever record? No, I never did. Never did record?
No.
In those days, I guess not very many musicians down here got a chance to record.
Got a chance for it, that's right. Just years late. Seeing my time coming up, I didn't get that chance.
It's too bad Chris Kelly didn't and Buddy Petey, none of those fellows made records. No, you didn't get that. Punch did and Armstrong and a lot of others. Yeah.
I think Punch only got that when he left here.
Yes, but Chicago, he made it.
